VulkanMod112

A Vulkan terrain renderer for Minecraft 1.12.2 Forge.

Minecraft keeps its window and its OpenGL context. VulkanMod112 mirrors the world's chunk geometry into Vulkan, draws the opaque terrain there, and hands the finished colour and depth back into the game's frame through shared GPU memory — no copy through system RAM, no second window.

What it draws

Vulkan takes the three opaque terrain layers. Water and glass, entities, block entities, particles, the sky and the interface are still drawn by the game's own OpenGL renderer, and everything lines up because the depth buffer is shared.

If Vulkan is missing, the driver lacks the extensions it needs, or anything at all goes wrong, the mod steps aside and the game renders exactly as it always did. Losing your world's visuals is never an acceptable outcome for a mod like this.

Beyond the renderer

The settings screen (Options → Video Settings → VulkanMod112 Settings…) also collects the things that actually decide a framerate in 1.12.2:

  • Entity and block-entity draw distances. Vanilla decides per object from its bounding box, which for large mobs reaches far past anything you can make out. This is the single biggest win in mob farms, storage rooms and busy servers.
  • Animated textures. Water, lava, fire, portals and every animated modded block upload a new frame every tick whether they are on screen or not.
  • Background framerate cap. With the frame limit on "unlimited", a minimised Minecraft otherwise keeps your GPU at full load drawing frames nobody can see.
  • Offscreen chunk preloading. The game only ever schedules a chunk rebuild for chunks that are on screen right now, so at high render distances the world fills in along whatever you are looking at. Off by default, and the setting tells you what it costs before you switch it on.
  • Hold-to-zoom, on C and rebindable, with mouse sensitivity scaled to match.
  • Render distance up to 64 chunks, for people who want to find out what their machine does with that.

Every setting states what it costs on the CPU, the GPU and in VRAM separately, because which of the three you are short of decides whether a setting will help you at all. Three presets — Stable, Balanced, Performance — are there if you would rather not read all of it, and Reset puts this mod's settings back without touching Minecraft's.

Requirements

  • Minecraft 1.12.2 with Forge
  • MixinBooter 10.7 or newer in your mods folder — a required dependency that no launcher installs for you
  • A 64-bit Vulkan driver on Windows or Linux, with the external-memory and external-semaphore extensions. Almost any driver from the last several years has them; without them the mod loads, says so, and leaves the terrain to OpenGL
  • Both OpenGL and Vulkan must land on the same GPU. On machines with more than one the mod compares device UUIDs at startup and stays on vanilla rendering if they differ, rather than crashing the way sharing memory across two devices otherwise would

Honest limits

This is not a drop-in OptiFine replacement, and it is not finished.

  • The world's geometry is stored twice while this is on: once in the game's OpenGL buffers and once in the Vulkan mirror. On a card without memory to spare, that is what limits how far you can push the render distance — and it depends on how much geometry is actually in view, not on the distance number by itself.
  • Chunk building dominates the frame while you move at high render distances. Every chunk gets uploaded twice, once by the game and once by this mod. Standing still is much faster than turning.
  • OptiFine and shader mods replace the same classes this mod does. When one is installed the Vulkan terrain simply is not loaded, and you get that renderer plus this mod's settings and game-side optimisations. They cannot share the terrain, and shader packs are a different project entirely.
  • No connected textures, no dynamic lighting, no shader packs.

Diagnostics

Turn on Ultra Logging in the settings screen and logs/vulkanmod112-diagnostics.log will record your versions, your installed mods, your GPU and driver, every active code path, the frame cost broken down between waiting, recording, submitting and the GPU itself, and the resource counters. Attach that file to a bug report and most questions answer themselves.
